questions.passage: To investigate whether contact with road surfaces changes the chemistry of snowmelt, a student collected samples during several winter melt events. table.caption: Average Chloride and Sodium Concentrations in Snowmelt Samples

questions.question: Which choice best describes the extent to which the student’s conclusion is supported by data from the table?

choices.A: The conclusion is challenged because the differences between chloride and sodium concentrations vary substantially among individual runoff events.
choices.B: The conclusion is supported only for bridge drainage because only those samples show elevated concentrations of both measured substances.
choices.C: The conclusion is strongly supported because both chloride and sodium concentrations are higher in every curb-runoff and bridge-drainage sample shown than in pristine snowmelt.

B is false because the curb-runoff samples also exceed the baseline for both substances. D is contradicted by the sodium values, which are far above 1.4 mg/L in every listed sample.

choiceExplanations.C: The baseline values for pristine snowmelt are only 2.3 mg/L chloride and 1.4 mg/L sodium. Every road-contact sample in the table substantially exceeds both values. That consistent pattern across both measured substances and both runoff types strongly supports the student’s conclusion.
choiceExplanations.A: A focuses on variation in the size of the increases, but such variation does not undermine the fact that all road-contact samples are elevated relative to the baseline.
choiceExplanations.B: B is false because the curb-runoff samples also exceed the baseline for both substances.
choiceExplanations.D: D is contradicted by the sodium values, which are far above 1.4 mg/L in every listed sample.

questions.passage: Regional climate models often represent mountain snowpack using grid cells several kilometers wide, even though snow depth can vary sharply over distances of only a few hundred meters. questions.passage: In traditional letterpress printing, experienced press operators often teach apprentices not only how to set type and regulate ink but also why pressure, paper moisture, and roller height must be adjusted for different jobs. _____ such as this helps ensure that practical knowledge accumulated through years of experience is transmitted to the next generation of printers.

D reverses the argument: the text distinguishes stronger evidence from weaker evidence rather than treating all sources as equally unreliable.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Attempts to classify historical maps automatically according to “cartographic schools” have produced inconsistent results. More fundamentally, historians Mirela Petrov and Daniel Cho question whether such categories are especially useful: workshops borrowed symbols, projections, lettering conventions, and decorative motifs from one another so extensively that labels such as “Venetian school” or “Dutch school” can conceal meaningful relationships among individual maps. Petrov and Cho argue that maps may sometimes be better compared through specific production practices than through broad school labels.
Text 2
Mediterranean portolan charts and some early Atlantic navigation charts share enough visual features that automated classification systems frequently confuse them. In a 2025 study, Amadou Keita and colleagues improved classification accuracy by converting maps into geometric feature networks and comparing recurring spatial relationships among coastlines, compass lines, and labels. questions.explanation:
Text 1 questions not merely the accuracy of classification but the usefulness of the categories themselves. Its authors argue that broad school labels can obscure meaningful connections among maps. They would therefore likely caution that even a technically improved classifier may offer limited benefit if the underlying categories remain reductive.
A may be true but does not address Text 2’s claim that improved classifications would benefit users. B is unsupported by either text. C conflicts with Text 1’s deeper concern: the problem is not simply that existing algorithms are imperfect but that the categories can themselves be misleading.

No October had opened so lucidly on the fen. Before sunrise, the channels reflected a hard silver sky; by eight, the mist had lifted from the reed beds in torn ribbons. Toward evening the cloudbank loosened, and copper light ran uninterrupted across the salt pools to the dunes.

Choice C best captures the passage’s purpose. Nearly every detail concerns the Marrow Fen itself: its channels, reed beds, clouds, salt pools, dunes, and changing light. The passage also emphasizes that this October differs from the region’s usual fogbound conditions, allowing the setting to be rendered through the progression from dawn to evening.
Choice A is unsupported because no difficulty or practical consequence results from the weather. Choice B is incorrect because no travelers or opposing forces appear. Choice D is tempting because the description is highly observant, but the passage never introduces an observer whose personality is being developed; the descriptive attention serves primarily to portray the place.

Engineers testing protective coatings for lithium-ion battery separators wanted to know whether reducing internal short circuits would necessarily improve a cell’s retained discharge capacity. Four coating systems were applied to otherwise identical batteries, which were then cycled 300 times. A lower short-circuit percentage indicates a more effective protective coating.

graph.caption: Battery Performance after 300 Charge Cycles

questions.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the underlined conclusion?

choices.A: the ceramic film produced a lower short-circuit rate than the oxide layer and was also associated with greater retained capacity.
choices.B: the polymer-brush and fluoropolymer coatings produced the two lowest short-circuit percentages, yet they were associated with the highest and lowest retained capacities, respectively.
choices.C: the oxide layer produced the greatest short-circuit percentage, whereas the polymer-brush coating produced the greatest retained capacity.
choices.D: the polymer-brush coating was associated with 94% retained capacity and only 3% short-circuited cells, outperforming the ceramic film on both measures.

questions.explanation:
B is correct. If more effective suppression of short circuits predictably produced greater retained capacity, the treatments with the lowest short-circuit rates should also tend to have the highest retained capacities. Instead, the two most effective coatings by short-circuit rate produce opposite extremes in capacity: the polymer brush has the highest retained capacity at 94%, while the nearly equally effective fluoropolymer film has the lowest at 56%. That contrast directly supports the conclusion that no predictable relationship exists.
A describes results consistent with a relationship in which better short-circuit suppression corresponds with greater capacity, so it does not support the claim of unpredictability. C compares two different extreme values but does not show why short-circuit effectiveness fails to predict capacity as clearly as B does. D also presents a result consistent with a positive relationship between the two measures rather than evidence against such a relationship.

questions.passage: In a study of how screen contrast affects proofreading efficiency, participants spent forty minutes on one day identifying typographical errors in passages displayed with relatively low contrast. However, lingering visual fatigue from the first session may have impaired participants’ performance during the second session. Thus, _____

choices.A: differences between the two sessions may have resulted primarily from participants becoming familiar with the proofreading task.
choices.B: researchers may have been unable to determine how many errors participants identified during the second session.
choices.C: the second session’s results may underestimate the extent to which higher contrast improves proofreading efficiency.
choices.D: participants likely preferred the higher-contrast display even if it did not improve their proofreading performance.

questions.explanation:

B is incorrect because nothing suggests that the researchers were unable to measure performance accurately. D is incorrect because the passage concerns proofreading efficiency, not participants’ subjective preferences.

questions.passage: Subglacial sediments contain diverse microorganisms, including the archaeon Nitrosopumilus glacialis and several species of heterotrophic bacteria, such as Polaromonas vacuolata. Researchers began with sediment samples whose microbial compositions were initially very similar, then subjected the samples to different oxygen concentrations and pressures. Both variables influenced microbial growth. However, when total archaeal growth increased, most of that increase was attributable specifically to N. glacialis, whereas changes in bacterial growth were distributed across numerous bacterial species.

table.caption: Growth Rates of Archaeal Communities in Three Subglacial Sediment Samples

questions.question: Taken together, the text and table best support which statement about the sediment samples at the conclusion of the experiment?

choices.A: The sample exposed to 16% oxygen and 2.5 atm necessarily contained a greater total proportion of archaea than of bacteria.
choices.B: The sample exposed to 8% oxygen and 1.0 atm contained a lower proportion of N. glacialis within its archaeal community than the sample exposed to 16% oxygen and 2.5 atm did.
choices.C: The sample exposed to 16% oxygen and 2.5 atm contained a greater proportion of N. glacialis than of P. vacuolata.
choices.D: The sample exposed to 8% oxygen and 1.0 atm contained a lower proportion of P. vacuolata than the sample exposed to 16% oxygen and 2.5 atm did.

questions.explanation:
The samples began with very similar microbial compositions. The table shows that archaeal growth was lowest under 8% oxygen and 1.0 atm and highest under 16% oxygen and 2.5 atm. The passage further states that increases in total archaeal growth were driven primarily by N. glacialis. It therefore follows that the condition producing much greater archaeal growth would also tend to produce a larger representation of N. glacialis within the archaeal community. Thus, the low-growth sample would contain a lower proportion of that archaeon than the high-growth sample, making B correct.
Choice A cannot be established because no data compare the total quantities of archaea and bacteria. Choice C also compares N. glacialis directly with a bacterial species, but neither the table nor the passage provides enough information to establish which species ultimately made up the larger proportion of the entire microbial community. Choice D is unsupported because the passage says bacterial growth changes were spread across many bacterial species; it does not single out P. vacuolata as varying systematically with the archaeal growth pattern.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from William Shakespeare’s play Measure for Measure, first performed around 1604. Duke Vincentio is reflecting on the consequences of having enforced Vienna’s laws too leniently.
DUKE:
For years I let the statutes sleep, preferring
Counsel to punishment when both were mine.
Habit has taught the insolent that restraint
Is but a threat rehearsed and never acted.
I know now what such lenity has purchased:
Not gratitude, but license to despise
The hand that would not govern. What I spared
Must now be ruled with firmer judgment.
questions.question: Which statement best describes how the Duke presents himself in the text?

choices.A: He admits that his reluctance to exercise authority has weakened respect for it and concludes that he must govern more forcefully.
choices.B: He argues that his measured treatment of offenders was fundamentally correct, even though others have mistaken restraint for weakness.
choices.C: He claims that he has judged wrongdoing impartially but recognizes that repeated punishment has nevertheless caused citizens to distrust him.
choices.D: He concedes that his administration has been ineffective, yet he attributes that failure primarily to the deliberate insolence of those subject to the law.

questions.explanation:
Choice A captures both parts of the Duke’s reasoning. He acknowledges that his own “lenity” and unwillingness to enforce the laws have taught people to disregard his authority, and he then states that what he previously spared “must now be ruled with firmer judgment.” He therefore sees his former tolerance as a cause of diminished respect and resolves to become more forceful.
Choice B contradicts the passage because the Duke does not defend his previous leniency; he identifies it as the source of the problem. Choice C reverses the situation: the Duke says he punished too little, not that excessive punishment caused distrust. Choice D contains part of the passage’s idea—the citizens have become insolent—but wrongly makes their behavior the primary cause. The Duke instead places responsibility on his own failure to enforce the law.

questions.passage: Hydrologists estimate snow-water equivalent (SWE), the amount of liquid water contained in a snowpack, using instruments such as snow pillows installed at monitoring stations. Because such stations are sparse in many high-elevation regions, researchers also estimate SWE remotely from satellite measurements of microwave radiation emitted and scattered by snow. The relationship between microwave signals and SWE varies with forest cover, snow-grain size, and liquid-water content, so the satellite measurement is not a direct substitute for an on-site reading. Nevertheless, studies have found that properly calibrated microwave observations often correspond closely with ground-based SWE measurements.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To explain why variation in forest cover prevents satellite measurements from providing meaningful estimates of mountain snowpack
choices.B: To compare two instruments that hydrologists commonly install at monitoring stations to determine which produces more reliable SWE measurements
choices.C: To describe a remotely obtained proxy for SWE that can partly address the limited geographic coverage of ground-based monitoring
choices.D: To identify systematic flaws in snow-pillow measurements that have led researchers to replace ground stations with satellite observations

questions.explanation:
Choice C accurately captures the passage as a whole. The text first establishes a limitation of the standard ground-based method: monitoring stations are sparse. It then introduces satellite microwave observations as an indirect way to estimate SWE across areas where ground measurements may be unavailable, while also acknowledging limitations in the relationship between the proxy and the quantity being measured.
Choice A exaggerates one complication into a complete failure; the text explicitly states that calibrated satellite observations often correspond well with ground measurements. Choice B is incorrect because the passage does not compare two ground instruments. Choice D misrepresents the motivation for the remote method: the problem described is insufficient geographic coverage, not systematic measurement error in snow pillows, and the text never says satellites have replaced ground stations.

- Because he cannot visually study a model while working, he learns the contours of many subjects through touch.
- He then relies on tactile and spatial memory as he shapes figures in clay.

questions.question: The student wants to describe Naranjo’s artistic process. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

Choice B merely identifies subjects he has depicted. Choice D provides biographical information and describes the subjects of his work but does not explain how he creates the sculptures.

questions.passage: Automated analysis of enormous collections of whale vocalizations allows bioacousticians to detect migration-scale patterns that would be difficult to recognize by examining recordings individually, but statistical aggregation can _____ the distinctive phrasing of particular animals. Close spectrographic study of single call sequences, by contrast, can reveal subtle variations that population-level summaries leave invisible.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: ratify
choices.B: elide
choices.C: magnify
choices.D: prefigure

questions.explanation:
Choice B, “elide,” means to omit, suppress, or pass over something. The passage contrasts broad statistical aggregation with close examination of individual calls. Because aggregation can make individual variations disappear from view, “elide” precisely expresses the intended idea.
Choice A, “ratify,” means to formally approve or confirm, which does not fit the relationship between statistical analysis and individual vocal patterns. Choice C, “magnify,” means to make something more prominent or noticeable, the opposite of what the next sentence suggests. Choice D, “prefigure,” means to foreshadow or anticipate something that comes later; nothing in the passage concerns prediction or foreshadowing.

Because aggregation can make individual variations disappear from view, “elide” precisely expresses the intended idea

questions.passage:
The following text is from Helena Marlowe’s 1907 play The Crown’s Measure. Governor Vale is addressing councilors who have repeatedly ignored his directives.
VALE:
I called my silence patience; you called it leave.
Because my hand lay quiet on the seal,
You thought the seal itself had lost its force.
Enough. I have worn courtesy so long
That even insolence mistakes it for surrender.
From this hour I will speak in my own voice,
And those who prized the softness of restraint
May learn what weight restraint was holding back.
questions.question: Which statement best describes how Vale presents himself in the text?

choices.A: He argues that his earlier restraint has been mistaken for weakness and resolves to reveal a more forceful aspect of his character.
choices.B: He admits that his harsh treatment of the councilors caused their defiance and promises to govern with greater patience.
choices.C: He maintains that courtesy is his most authentic trait and insists that he will preserve it even if the councilors continue to disregard him.
choices.D: He claims that the councilors have obeyed him too readily and therefore urges them to challenge his authority more openly.

choiceExplanations.A: Vale says that his “silence” and “courtesy” have been interpreted as permission, surrender, or lack of force. He then declares that he will now “speak in my own voice” and reveal the “weight” that restraint had concealed. Thus, A accurately captures both parts of his self-presentation: he believes his earlier restraint damaged perceptions of his authority, and he now intends to act more forcefully.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice reverses the situation; Vale does not say he has been excessively harsh.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice contradicts his decision to stop relying on the softness of restraint.
choiceExplanations.D: This choice is unsupported because the councilors have been insufficiently deferential, not excessively obedient.

questions.explanation: Vale says that his “silence” and “courtesy” have been interpreted as permission, surrender, or lack of force. He then declares that he will now “speak in my own voice” and reveal the “weight” that restraint had concealed. Thus, A accurately captures both parts of his self-presentation: he believes his earlier restraint damaged perceptions of his authority, and he now intends to act more forcefully. B reverses the situation; Vale does not say he has been excessively harsh. C contradicts his decision to stop relying on the softness of restraint. D is unsupported because the councilors have been insufficiently deferential, not excessively obedient.

questions.passage: From the pallid bat to the greater mouse-eared bat, several distantly related species make long nightly trips between roosts and feeding grounds. choices.B: To describe a flight pattern that explains why certain bats use less energy than all other nocturnal mammals
choices.C: To identify a behavioral similarity among several bat species that makes protecting them unusually difficult

choiceExplanations.C: This choice incorrectly characterizes the shared behavior as an obstacle to conservation; the text instead suggests that understanding the pattern could assist conservation.
choiceExplanations.D: The passage presents a research finding about where several bat species tend to fly during long-distance commuting and then explains a possible conservation application: the information could help determine where turbine restrictions would most effectively reduce collisions.

questions.passage: Printing workshops established in Iceland during the late nineteenth century tended to rely on comparatively modest equipment. questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
Bombardier beetles possess abdominal glands that store chemicals used in a defensive reaction.
When threatened, the beetles can combine the chemicals and eject a hot, irritating spray.
The spray can cause an attacking predator to release or retreat from the beetle.
The beetles do not normally use this chemical spray to capture prey.
questions.question: The student wants to explain how bombardier beetles use their chemical reaction for protection. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Bombardier beetles can eject a hot, irritating chemical spray that causes attacking predators to release them or retreat.
choices.B: Bombardier beetles store the chemicals involved in their defensive reaction in abdominal glands.
choices.C: Bombardier beetles combine chemicals immediately before producing their characteristic spray.
choices.D: Bombardier beetles generally do not rely on their chemical spray when capturing prey.

choiceExplanations.A: It directly explains both the defensive behavior and its protective effect: the beetle releases an irritating spray, and the spray can cause a predator to let go or withdraw.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice does not work because it explains where the chemicals are stored but not how the reaction protects the beetle. C describes part of the mechanism behind the spray but does not state how the spray affects a predator. D distinguishes defense from hunting but still does not explain the protective mechanism itself.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice describes part of the mechanism behind the spray but does not state how the spray affects a predator.
choiceExplanations.D: This choice distinguishes defense from hunting but still does not explain the protective mechanism itself.

questions.explanation: It directly explains both the defensive behavior and its protective effect: the beetle releases an irritating spray, and the spray can cause a predator to let go or withdraw.

questions.passage: H. G. Wells’s 1895 novel The Time Machine presents a discussion in which the Time Traveller argues that time should be understood as a dimension comparable in an important respect to the dimensions of space. _____
questions.question: Which quotation from The Time Machine most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.A: “The whole surface of the earth seemed changed—melting and flowing under my eyes.”
choices.B: “I gripped the lever with both hands, and went off with a thud.”
choices.C: “The laboratory got hazy and went dark.”
choices.D: “There is no difference between Time and any of the three dimensions of Space except that our consciousness moves along it.”

choiceExplanations.A: This choice describes the appearance of Earth changing as the narrator moves through time; although related to time travel, it does not directly support the specific claim about the dimensional nature of time.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice does not work because it describes the operation of the time machine rather than the theoretical relationship between time and space. C describes a visual effect experienced during time travel but offers no conceptual explanation of time as a dimension. D describes the appearance of Earth changing as the narrator moves through time; although related to time travel, it does not directly support the specific claim about the dimensional nature of time.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice describes a visual effect experienced during time travel but offers no conceptual explanation of time as a dimension.
choiceExplanations.D: The claim concerns the Time Traveller’s argument that time is a dimension comparable to spatial dimensions.

questions.explanation: The claim concerns the Time Traveller’s argument that time is a dimension comparable to spatial dimensions. Choice A states this idea directly by comparing Time with “the three dimensions of Space” and identifying consciousness as the relevant difference.

questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: would painters working on major commissions before then have reserved natural ultramarine for particularly important passages?
choices.B: painters working on major commissions before then would often have reserved natural ultramarine for particularly important passages?
choices.C: would painters working on major commissions before then have reserved natural ultramarine for particularly important passages.
choices.D: painters working on major commissions before then would often have reserved natural ultramarine for particularly important passages.

choiceExplanations.A: This choice does not work because it uses inverted question word order (“would painters ... have reserved”) and ends with a question mark, even though the introductory phrase sets up a statement. B uses the correct declarative word order but incorrectly ends the sentence with a question mark. C uses interrogative word order but ends with a period; changing the punctuation does not make the inverted structure appropriate for the declarative sentence.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice uses the correct declarative word order but incorrectly ends the sentence with a question mark.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice uses interrogative word order but ends with a period; changing the punctuation does not make the inverted structure appropriate for the declarative sentence.
choiceExplanations.D: The introductory phrase “According to conservation historians,” is followed by a declarative statement. Therefore, the sentence requires normal subject-verb order: “painters ... would often have reserved...” Since it is a statement rather than a question, it must end with a period.

Therefore, the sentence requires normal subject-verb order: “painters ... would often have reserved...” Since it is a statement rather than a question, it must end with a period.

questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: 1987, there
choices.B: 1987 there
choices.C: 1987. There
choices.D: 1987, and there

choiceExplanations.A: The clause beginning with “If” is a dependent clause: “If a horticulturist had inspected commercial greenhouses during the winter of 1987.” It cannot stand alone as a complete sentence. When an introductory dependent clause precedes the independent clause it modifies, a comma should separate the two: “1987, there was a strong chance....”
choiceExplanations.B: Choice

choiceExplanations.D: This choice unnecessarily inserts the coordinating conjunction “and.” The relationship between the clauses is already established by “If,” so the sentence requires only a comma.

When an introductory dependent clause precedes the independent clause it modifies, a comma should separate the two: “1987, there was a strong chance....”

questions.passage: In a 1911 paper interpreting the results of gold-foil experiments, physicist Ernest Rutherford proposed that nearly all of an atom’s positive charge was concentrated in a minute central region called the _____ interpretation fundamentally altered prevailing models of atomic structure.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: nucleus, Rutherford’s
choices.B: nucleus Rutherford’s
choices.C: nucleus and Rutherford’s
choices.D: nucleus. Rutherford’s

choiceExplanations.A: This choice creates a comma splice because it joins two independent clauses with only a comma.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice provides no punctuation at all between the two independent clauses, producing a run-on sentence.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice uses “and,” but without the comma normally needed before a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses; moreover, its construction awkwardly makes “Rutherford’s interpretation” appear to continue the object of “called.” Only C establishes a clear sentence boundary.
choiceExplanations.D: The text contains two independent clauses: “physicist Ernest Rutherford proposed that nearly all of an atom’s positive charge was concentrated in a minute central region called the nucleus” and “Rutherford’s interpretation fundamentally altered prevailing models of atomic structure.” A period correctly separates those two complete thoughts.

questions.explanation:
The text contains two independent clauses: “physicist Ernest Rutherford proposed that nearly all of an atom’s positive charge was concentrated in a minute central region called the nucleus” and “Rutherford’s interpretation fundamentally altered prevailing models of atomic structure.” A period correctly separates those two complete thoughts.
Choice A creates a comma splice because it joins two independent clauses with only a comma. Choice B provides no punctuation at all between the two independent clauses, producing a run-on sentence. Choice D uses “and,” but without the comma normally needed before a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses; moreover, its construction awkwardly makes “Rutherford’s interpretation” appear to continue the object of “called.” Only C establishes a clear sentence boundary.

questions.passage: Although the Pratt truss was widely adopted for railroad bridges during the nineteenth century, it receives relatively little attention in popular histories of structural engineering, a literature often centered on a handful of monumental suspension-bridge _____ that narrow narrative, historian Celeste Navarro has documented how standardized truss designs transformed regional freight networks.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: projects, and reassessing
choices.B: projects, reassessing
choices.C: projects reassessing
choices.D: projects. Reassessing

choiceExplanations.A: This choice does not solve the problem: the conjunction “and” cannot appropriately attach the participial phrase “reassessing that narrow narrative” to the preceding noun phrase while also introducing the new subject “historian Celeste Navarro.”
choiceExplanations.B: This choice incorrectly joins the complete first sentence to a second independent clause with only a comma.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice supplies no boundary at all and also momentarily suggests that the “projects” themselves are “reassessing” something.
choiceExplanations.D: The first sentence forms a complete thought ending with “suspension-bridge projects.” The next sentence begins with the introductory participial phrase “Reassessing that narrow narrative,” which appropriately modifies the subject “historian Celeste Navarro.” A period is therefore needed before “Reassessing.”

questions.explanation: The first sentence forms a complete thought ending with “suspension-bridge projects.” The next sentence begins with the introductory participial phrase “Reassessing that narrow narrative,” which appropriately modifies the subject “historian Celeste Navarro.” A period is therefore needed before “Reassessing.”

questions.passage: Crystalline diamond transmits heat considerably more efficiently than ordinary window glass _____ phonon scattering, the process by which lattice vibrations are disrupted by defects or boundaries, helps determine how readily thermal energy moves through a solid.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: does. Phonon scattering,
choices.B: does. Phonon scattering—which is
choices.C: does. Phonon scattering is
choices.D: does, phonon scattering,

choiceExplanations.A: “Crystalline diamond transmits heat considerably more efficiently than ordinary window glass does” is a complete sentence. The next sentence has “phonon scattering” as its subject and “helps determine” as its main verb. The phrase “the process by which lattice vibrations are disrupted by defects or boundaries” is a nonessential appositive explaining what phonon scattering is, so it is correctly enclosed by commas.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice begins a parenthetical construction with a dash but never closes it before the main verb “helps.” Choice C creates competing main predicates: “Phonon scattering is the process...” and “helps determine....” Because “is” makes the intervening material part of the main clause rather than an appositive, the sentence cannot grammatically proceed to “helps determine.” Only D produces two complete, correctly structured sentences.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice begins a parenthetical construction with a dash but never closes it before the main verb “helps.” Choice C creates competing main predicates: “Phonon scattering is the process...” and “helps determine....” Because “is” makes the intervening material part of the main clause rather than an appositive, the sentence cannot grammatically proceed to “helps determine.” Only D produces two complete, correctly structured sentences.
choiceExplanations.D: This choice uses only a comma to join two independent clauses, creating a comma splice.

questions.explanation:
“Crystalline diamond transmits heat considerably more efficiently than ordinary window glass does” is a complete sentence. The next sentence has “phonon scattering” as its subject and “helps determine” as its main verb. The phrase “the process by which lattice vibrations are disrupted by defects or boundaries” is a nonessential appositive explaining what phonon scattering is, so it is correctly enclosed by commas.
Choice A uses only a comma to join two independent clauses, creating a comma splice. Choice B begins a parenthetical construction with a dash but never closes it before the main verb “helps.” Choice C creates competing main predicates: “Phonon scattering is the process...” and “helps determine....” Because “is” makes the intervening material part of the main clause rather than an appositive, the sentence cannot grammatically proceed to “helps determine.” Only D produces two complete, correctly structured sentences.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
John James Audubon’s The Birds of America was published in installments between 1827 and 1838.
The completed work contains 435 hand-colored plates depicting birds.
The plates were printed on sheets measuring approximately 39 by 26 inches.
This unusually large page size is known as “double-elephant folio.”
The large format allowed Audubon to portray many species at or near life size.
questions.question: The student wants to describe the physical format of The Birds of America. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Audubon selected an unusually large page size so that many of the birds in The Birds of America could be shown at or near life size.
choices.B: Nineteenth-century natural-history publications were commonly produced on double-elephant folio sheets large enough to accommodate life-size illustrations.
choices.C: Published in installments from 1827 through 1838, The Birds of America eventually included hundreds of hand-colored depictions of birds.
choices.D: The Birds of America contains 435 hand-colored plates printed on approximately 39-by-26-inch sheets in a format known as double-elephant folio.

choiceExplanations.A: This choice focuses primarily on why Audubon chose the format rather than describing the format itself.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice makes an unsupported generalization about nineteenth-century natural-history publications; the notes establish that The Birds of America used this format, not that such a format was common across the field.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice emphasizes publication history and the contents of the work but omits the defining physical information about page dimensions and double-elephant folio size.
choiceExplanations.D: This choice works because it directly describes the work’s physical format. It identifies both the number and nature of the plates and, crucially, the approximate dimensions and name of the large folio format.

questions.explanation:
This choice works because it directly describes the work’s physical format. It identifies both the number and nature of the plates and, crucially, the approximate dimensions and name of the large folio format.
Choice A focuses primarily on why Audubon chose the format rather than describing the format itself. Choice C emphasizes publication history and the contents of the work but omits the defining physical information about page dimensions and double-elephant folio size. Choice D makes an unsupported generalization about nineteenth-century natural-history publications; the notes establish that The Birds of America used this format, not that such a format was common across the field.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
The Svalbard Global Seed Vault opened on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen in 2008.
The vault stores backup copies of seed samples held by gene banks around the world.
The Nordic Genetic Resource Center, known as NordGen, is one of the organizations involved in the vault’s operation.
NordGen receives incoming seed deposits and maintains records identifying the deposited material.
The Crop Trust helps support the conservation system financially.
The vault was designed to protect crop diversity from losses caused by disasters, conflict, equipment failures, and other threats.
questions.question: The student wants to provide an example of a responsibility NordGen performs in connection with the Svalbard Global Seed Vault. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Because disasters and equipment failures can threaten gene-bank collections, backup seed samples are stored at Svalbard.
choices.B: Opened in 2008 on Spitsbergen, the Svalbard Global Seed Vault preserves backup samples from gene banks around the world.
choices.C: NordGen and the Crop Trust both contribute to an international system intended to reduce the risk that crop diversity will be permanently lost.
choices.D: NordGen receives seed deposits sent to the Svalbard Global Seed Vault and maintains records identifying the stored material.

choiceExplanations.A: This choice explains the purpose of storing backup seeds but says nothing about NordGen’s role.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice describes the Seed Vault itself rather than a responsibility performed by NordGen.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice mentions NordGen but gives only a broad statement about participation in the conservation system; it does not identify a particular responsibility that NordGen carries out.
choiceExplanations.D: This choice works because it provides a concrete example of a task specifically attributed to NordGen: receiving incoming deposits and maintaining information about them. It therefore directly fulfills the student’s goal of identifying one of NordGen’s responsibilities.

questions.explanation:
This choice works because it provides a concrete example of a task specifically attributed to NordGen: receiving incoming deposits and maintaining information about them. It therefore directly fulfills the student’s goal of identifying one of NordGen’s responsibilities.
Choice B describes the Seed Vault itself rather than a responsibility performed by NordGen. Choice C mentions NordGen but gives only a broad statement about participation in the conservation system; it does not identify a particular responsibility that NordGen carries out. Choice D explains the purpose of storing backup seeds but says nothing about NordGen’s role.

questions.passage: A shift from centralized workshop production to more dispersed household manufacture in the Koru Valley between approximately 900 and 600 BCE can be inferred from ceramic remains in settlements dating to different periods. Vessels from layers dating to about 900 BCE are generally <u>highly standardized in diameter, stamped with one of only three workshop seals, and made from clay originating near the valley’s fortified administrative center</u>. Pottery from layers younger than about 650 BCE, however, <u>varies much more widely in size, bears dozens of distinct local marks, and incorporates clay from several separate tributary valleys</u>.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the two underlined portions in the text as a whole?

choices.A: They describe differing characteristics of earlier and later pottery that together support the claim that production became less centralized and more locally varied over time.
choices.B: They provide evidence from two periods that supports the claim that ceramic production remained concentrated near the Koru Valley’s administrative center.
choices.C: They distinguish pottery from separate geographical regions in order to suggest that different communities simultaneously adopted incompatible manufacturing traditions.
choices.D: They identify contrasting features of pottery assemblages that together suggest that the overall amount of ceramic production declined steadily during the period discussed.

choiceExplanations.A: The first underlined portion describes uniformity and centralization: standardized sizes, only three workshop seals, and clay from near the administrative center. The second describes greater variation and geographic dispersion: wider differences in size, many local marks, and clay from multiple valleys. Taken together, those contrasts support the passage’s opening claim that production shifted from centralized workshops toward more dispersed local manufacture.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice contradicts the younger evidence, which points away from continued concentration near the administrative center.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice incorrectly treats the evidence primarily as a simultaneous geographical comparison; the passage explicitly contrasts assemblages from different periods to establish change over time.
choiceExplanations.D: Choice

questions.explanation: The first underlined portion describes uniformity and centralization: standardized sizes, only three workshop seals, and clay from near the administrative center. The second describes greater variation and geographic dispersion: wider differences in size, many local marks, and clay from multiple valleys. Taken together, those contrasts support the passage’s opening claim that production shifted from centralized workshops toward more dispersed local manufacture.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
The Niagara Movement was a civil rights organization formed in 1905 by Black activists demanding full political and civil equality in the United States.
W.E.B. Du Bois and William Monroe Trotter were among its principal organizers.
Twenty-nine activists attended an organizational meeting in July 1905 at Fort Erie, Ontario, near Niagara Falls.
Members advocated voting rights, equal economic opportunity, and an end to racial segregation.
The movement rejected strategies that accepted racial inequality in exchange for gradual economic advancement.
Several participants later helped establish the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) in 1909.
questions.question: The student wants to begin a narrative about the Niagara Movement. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: W.E.B. Du Bois and William Monroe Trotter established the NAACP at Fort Erie in 1905 after twenty-nine activists endorsed a program of gradual economic advancement.
choices.B: By 1909, several people associated with the Niagara Movement had helped establish the NAACP, extending the struggle for civil rights through a new organization.
choices.C: Political equality rarely develops without sustained disagreement, organization, and pressure from people dissatisfied with existing institutions.
choices.D: In July 1905, twenty-nine Black activists gathered at Fort Erie near Niagara Falls; from that meeting would emerge the Niagara Movement and its campaign for full civil and political equality.

choiceExplanations.A: This choice contains multiple inaccuracies: the notes do not say that Du Bois and Trotter established the NAACP at Fort Erie in 1905, and the Niagara Movement rejected rather than endorsed acceptance of inequality in exchange for gradual advancement.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice accurately uses information from the notes, but it jumps ahead to a later consequence in 1909; it would work better near the end of a narrative than at its beginning.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice offers a broad generalization about political change rather than beginning the particular story described in the notes.
choiceExplanations.D:
This choice works because it functions naturally as the beginning of a narrative. It establishes a specific time and place, introduces the people involved in the opening event, and points forward to what their gathering would become. That chronological setup creates a clear starting point from which a narrative can proceed.

questions.passage: The following text is from Walt Whitman’s 1855 poem Song of Myself. The speaker acknowledges that apparently incompatible qualities or beliefs can coexist within a single person, suggesting that such inconsistency does not diminish the complexity of the self. _____
questions.question: Which quotation from Song of Myself most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.A: “I celebrate myself, and sing myself, / And what I assume you shall assume”
choices.B: “I too am not a bit tamed, I too am untranslatable, / I sound my barbaric yawp over the roofs of the world.”
choices.C: “I loafe and invite my soul, / I lean and loafe at my ease observing a spear of summer grass.”
choices.D: “Do I contradict myself? / Very well then I contradict myself, / (I am large, I contain multitudes.)”

choiceExplanations.A: This choice emphasizes identification between the speaker and others, not the coexistence of contradictory qualities within the speaker.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice emphasizes the speaker’s untamed and difficult-to-define nature, which could suggest individuality, but it does not directly address the acceptance of contradiction as B does.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice depicts contemplation and leisure but says nothing about inconsistency or complexity of identity.
choiceExplanations.D: The claim concerns the speaker’s acceptance of internal inconsistency as part of a complex identity. In B, the speaker explicitly acknowledges that he may “contradict” himself and immediately explains that contradiction by saying he “contain[s] multitudes.” The quotation therefore directly supports both parts of the claim: inconsistency exists, and that inconsistency reflects expansiveness rather than deficiency.

questions.explanation:
The claim concerns the speaker’s acceptance of internal inconsistency as part of a complex identity. In B, the speaker explicitly acknowledges that he may “contradict” himself and immediately explains that contradiction by saying he “contain[s] multitudes.” The quotation therefore directly supports both parts of the claim: inconsistency exists, and that inconsistency reflects expansiveness rather than deficiency.
A emphasizes identification between the speaker and others, not the coexistence of contradictory qualities within the speaker. C depicts contemplation and leisure but says nothing about inconsistency or complexity of identity. D emphasizes the speaker’s untamed and difficult-to-define nature, which could suggest individuality, but it does not directly address the acceptance of contradiction as B does.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Sarah Orne Jewett’s 1896 novel The Country of the Pointed Firs. The narrator has recently arrived in a small coastal settlement in Maine.
Beyond the clustered roofs, the harbor widened toward a chain of low islands whose dark spruce trees seemed almost level with the sea. At high tide, the water reached the weathered pilings beneath the wharves; when it withdrew, broad beds of rockweed shone between exposed stones. The afternoon wind carried salt through the open windows, while fishing boats, diminished by distance, moved slowly across the pale outer bay.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To establish the physical character and atmosphere of a coastal setting
choices.B: To introduce a disagreement between the narrator and the fishing community
choices.C: To explain an economic difficulty confronting the settlement’s residents
choices.D: To characterize the narrator through a decision the narrator is preparing to make

choiceExplanations.A: Nearly every detail concerns the surrounding environment: the harbor, islands, spruce trees, tides, wharves, rockweed, salt air, and distant fishing boats. Together, these details create a vivid impression of the coastal landscape and its atmosphere.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice does not work because no disagreement or conflict appears.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice does not work because the text does not discuss income, trade, scarcity, or any other economic problem.
choiceExplanations.D: This choice does not work because although the narrator observes the setting, the passage does not reveal a decision, plan, or significant personality trait. Its focus is overwhelmingly on place rather than plot or characterization.

questions.explanation: Nearly every detail concerns the surrounding environment: the harbor, islands, spruce trees, tides, wharves, rockweed, salt air, and distant fishing boats. Together, these details create a vivid impression of the coastal landscape and its atmosphere.

choices.A: examine:

questions.passage: Engineers investigating lower-carbon paving materials tested whether finely crushed basalt could replace part of the mineral filler in a composite without substantially reducing its flexural strength. Four mixtures were prepared: a baseline mixture with no basalt substitution and mixtures containing 8%, 16%, or 32% basalt. Flexural strength was measured after 10 and 30 days of curing. Based on the results, the researchers recommended using basalt substitutions of approximately 8% when maintaining structural strength is a priority.
questions.question: Which choice most effectively uses the data shown to support the researchers’ recommendation?

choices.A: The 8% basalt mixture never exceeded the flexural strength of the baseline mixture at either measurement point.
choices.B: The flexural strength of the 8% basalt mixture changed very little between day 10 and day 30, whereas the strengths of the 16% and 32% mixtures increased over the same interval.
choices.C: The 8% basalt mixture was stronger than the baseline mixture on day 10, but by day 30 its strength had declined while that of the baseline mixture had increased.
choices.D: The 8% basalt mixture equaled or exceeded the baseline mixture in flexural strength on both measurement days, whereas the 16% and 32% mixtures remained below the baseline on both days.

choiceExplanations.A: This choice is false because the 8% mixture exceeds the baseline on day 10.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice accurately notices that the 8% value changes little, but stability alone does not establish that its strength remains comparable to the baseline; C provides the more relevant comparison.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice does not work because the 8% mixture does not decline between the two measurements; it rises slightly.
choiceExplanations.D: On day 10, the 8% mixture has a flexural strength of about 44 MPa, compared with about 42 MPa for the baseline. On day 30, the 8% mixture is about 45 MPa, essentially equal to the baseline’s 45 MPa. By contrast, both the 16% and 32% mixtures remain substantially weaker than the baseline at both measurements. These data directly support recommending the smaller substitution level when strength must be preserved.

questions.explanation:
On day 10, the 8% mixture has a flexural strength of about 44 MPa, compared with about 42 MPa for the baseline. On day 30, the 8% mixture is about 45 MPa, essentially equal to the baseline’s 45 MPa. By contrast, both the 16% and 32% mixtures remain substantially weaker than the baseline at both measurements. These data directly support recommending the smaller substitution level when strength must be preserved.
A is false because the 8% mixture exceeds the baseline on day 10. B accurately notices that the 8% value changes little, but stability alone does not establish that its strength remains comparable to the baseline; C provides the more relevant comparison.

questions.passage: Producing exceptionally large scholarly reference books requires publishers to balance legibility, binding durability, and manufacturing cost. One recent botanical compendium contains approximately 460,800 words across 1,280 pages, while a comparative atlas of marine invertebrates contains about 604,800 words in a 960-page edition. This suggests that _____
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the marine-invertebrate atlas contains more words per page than the botanical compendium does.
choices.B: the botanical compendium was probably less expensive to manufacture than the marine-invertebrate atlas.
choices.C: the botanical compendium likely contained fewer words before it was edited for publication.
choices.D: readers would require approximately the same amount of time to finish the two works.

choiceExplanations.A: The botanical compendium averages 460,8001,280=360 words per page. The marine-invertebrate atlas averages 604,800960=630 words per page. Therefore, the atlas contains substantially more words per page.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice is unsupported because page and word counts alone do not establish manufacturing costs; paper quality, illustrations, binding, print run, and other factors could matter.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice cannot be inferred because no information is given about earlier drafts.
choiceExplanations.D: This choice is also unsupported: reading time depends on far more than page count, and the works differ considerably in total word count.

questions.explanation:

questions.passage: In 2021, historian Nadia Farouk published Beyond the Last Meridian, a biography of surveyor and expedition leader Elias Venn. The book recounts major episodes in Venn’s life, including his mapping of the Arken Plateau, his negotiations with rival survey teams, and his early apprenticeship under instrument maker Paolo Serrin. Yet Farouk organizes those episodes backward: the book opens with Venn’s final expedition and gradually retreats toward his adolescence. Reviewing the biography, critic Hana Okafor wrote that this arrangement “turns causation into an afterthought; the reader repeatedly encounters consequences before being allowed to understand their origins.”
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It contrasts two biographies of the same historical figure before explaining why one biography received stronger reviews.
choices.B: It introduces the subject of a biography, summarizes major events from that person’s life, and argues that the biography omits important causes of those events.
choices.C: It describes an unconventional feature of a biography, explains why the biographer selected that feature, and then defends the feature against a critic’s objection.
choices.D: It identifies a biography, notes several events that the biography covers, and then presents a critic’s negative assessment of one aspect of the biography’s organization.

choiceExplanations.A: Choice
choiceExplanations.B: This choice mischaracterizes the criticism: Okafor criticizes the order in which causes and consequences are presented, not the omission of causes from the biography altogether.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice correctly recognizes that the organization is unconventional but incorrectly claims that the passage explains why Farouk chose it and then defends the decision. Neither occurs.
choiceExplanations.D: The passage first identifies Farouk’s biography of Elias Venn. It then lists several episodes from Venn’s life that the biography covers. Finally, it explains the book’s reverse chronology and provides Okafor’s criticism of that organizational choice. Choice D accurately captures all three stages.

questions.passage: In competitive orchid breeding, exhibition labels often include lineage diagrams, provenance notes, and hand-rendered sketches that reflect growers’ priorities and classification habits. ____ many breeders spend considerable time preparing these displays, treating them not merely as identification cards but as integral parts of how a specimen is presented.

choices.B: Nevertheless,
choices.C: Consequently,
choices.D: Finally,

Saying that breeders devote substantial time to the displays and regard them as integral to presenting a specimen provides further evidence for that idea, so “Indeed” appropriately signals emphasis and confirmation.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice does not work because “Nevertheless” signals a contrast, but the second sentence supports rather than contradicts the first.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice does not work because “Consequently” would indicate that the time spent preparing labels is a result of the specific features listed in the first sentence; the relationship is primarily one of reinforcement, not cause and effect.
choiceExplanations.D: This choice does not work because “Finally” signals the last step in a sequence, and no sequence of steps has been established.

questions.explanation: This choice. Indeed, is correct. The second sentence reinforces the first sentence’s suggestion that exhibition labels are meaningful expressions of a breeder’s priorities. Saying that breeders devote substantial time to the displays and regard them as integral to presenting a specimen provides further evidence for that idea, so “Indeed” appropriately signals emphasis and confirmation.

questions.passage: During the 1970s, fluorescent yellow tennis balls increasingly displaced white ones in televised tournaments. choices.C: leading

choiceExplanations.A: This choice does not work because “having led” is a participial construction and cannot serve as the finite main verb here.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice does not work because “which led” would create another subordinate relative clause and leave the sentence without a main verb.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice does not work because “leading” is also a participle rather than the required finite verb.
choiceExplanations.D: This choice. led is correct. The subject of the sentence is “The sport’s widespread adoption of the brighter color.” Although the intervening relative clause beginning with “which” contains its own verb, the main clause still requires a finite verb. “Led” supplies that verb: “The sport’s widespread adoption . . . led to television producers favoring it.”

The subject of the sentence is “The sport’s widespread adoption of the brighter color.” Although the intervening relative clause beginning with “which” contains its own verb, the main clause still requires a finite verb. “Led” supplies that verb: “The sport’s widespread adoption . . . led to television producers favoring it.”

For years my notebooks had been crowded with calculations that seemed to terminate in other calculations: predicted currents, sediment estimates, revisions to earlier estimates. On the marsh, however, each measurement governed some tangible decision—where a channel would be reopened, how high a barrier would stand, whether young cordgrass would survive the next spring tide. After so much work that had existed chiefly on paper, my figures had acquired a practical end.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does the word “end” most nearly mean?

choices.B: consequence
choices.C: boundary

choiceExplanations.C: This choice does not work because end can mean a physical or temporal boundary, but nothing in the passage concerns the boundary of the calculations.
choiceExplanations.D: This choice does not work because end can also mean termination, but the calculations have not merely stopped; they have gained a practical purpose.

questions.explanation: This choice. objective is correct. The passage contrasts calculations that previously seemed abstract with calculations that now serve a concrete practical purpose. In the phrase “a practical end,” end therefore means an aim, purpose, or objective.

A historical exhibition never merely accumulates surviving objects. questions.passage: A 2022 paper by Priya Nandakumar and colleagues introduced nanoscale infrared mapping (NIM), a method that simultaneously images microscopic structures and identifies chemical bonds within them. Researchers led by Mateo Ruiz later combined NIM with expansion microscopy, in which a swellable polymer physically enlarges a prepared specimen. The resulting technique, expansion-assisted nanoscale infrared mapping (eNIM), preserves NIM’s chemical-identification capabilities while reducing the spatial-resolution limitation by increasing the physical separation between neighboring structures.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It introduces an analytical technique, explains a limitation of that technique, describes how researchers incorporated another method to produce a new technique, and identifies an advantage of the resulting approach.
choices.B: It describes two independently developed microscopy techniques, compares the scientific questions each is designed to answer, and argues that one should replace the other.
choices.C: It introduces a newer imaging technique that corrects flaws in an earlier method and then explains that the same researchers originally developed both techniques.
choices.D: It explains the principal function of expansion microscopy, describes evidence that the technique performs poorly in chemical analysis, and proposes combining it with conventional light microscopy.

choiceExplanations.A: This choice accurately follows the passage’s progression. The text first introduces NIM and its function, then identifies its spatial-resolution limitation. choiceExplanations.B: This choice incorrectly says the two techniques are merely compared as independent alternatives; the passage instead explains that they are combined.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice incorrectly claims the same researchers developed both the original and newer techniques.
choiceExplanations.D: This choice reverses the passage’s emphasis: the text does not present expansion microscopy as chemically inadequate or propose combining it with ordinary light microscopy.

questions.passage: At pressures millions of times greater than atmospheric pressure, water can enter a phase known as superionic ice, whose behavior complicates the conventional distinction between solids and liquids. questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Edith Wharton’s 1905 novel The House of Mirth. Lily Bart has received an unexpected act of consideration from a person whose motives she had previously distrusted.
Lily was more deeply touched by the unexpected kindness than she wished him to perceive; for a moment the practiced lightness of her manner deserted her, and the answer she had prepared seemed suddenly inadequate.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does the word “touched” most nearly mean?

choices.A: physically contacted
choices.B: reached after difficulty
choices.C: affected emotionally
choices.D: altered superficially

choiceExplanations.A: This choice uses the literal physical meaning of “touched,” but no physical contact is described.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice uses “touched” in the sense of reaching a location or point, which does not fit the context.
choiceExplanations.C: ” The kindness changes Lily’s emotional state: her usual manner momentarily deserts her, and the response she had prepared no longer seems adequate. Thus, “touched” means emotionally moved or affected.
choiceExplanations.D: This choice suggests a minor external alteration, whereas the passage describes an internal emotional reaction.

questions.explanation:
” The kindness changes Lily’s emotional state: her usual manner momentarily deserts her, and the response she had prepared no longer seems adequate. Thus, “touched” means emotionally moved or affected.
A uses the literal physical meaning of “touched,” but no physical contact is described. C uses “touched” in the sense of reaching a location or point, which does not fit the context. D suggests a minor external alteration, whereas the passage describes an internal emotional reaction.

questions.passage: Landscape architect Mireya Solano’s Tide Court allows seawater to enter a public plaza through concealed channels, periodically transforming dry stone terraces into shallow reflective pools. Because the pumps and gates remain hidden, visitors infer the hydraulic system from the plaza’s changing condition rather than seeing the machinery itself. Engineer-artist Anton Bell’s Waterworks Pavilion, by contrast, places its valves, pipes, gauges, and filtration tanks in full view; visitors can watch water moving through the structure while standing inside it. Both projects encourage attention to infrastructure that urban landscapes ordinarily conceal.
questions.question: Based on the text, which choice best describes how Solano’s and Bell’s approaches differ?

choices.A: Both direct attention to water-control infrastructure, but Solano does so indirectly while Bell exposes the relevant mechanisms explicitly.
choices.B: Both emphasize the artificiality of engineered landscapes, but Solano celebrates that artificiality whereas Bell condemns it.
choices.C: Both create hydraulic events that could not occur outside an artwork, but Solano conceals the process while Bell records it for visitors.
choices.D: Both employ sophisticated water systems, but Solano uses hers to imitate untouched nature whereas Bell rejects naturalistic representation.

choiceExplanations.A: Both projects draw visitors’ attention to infrastructure. Solano’s project does this implicitly: visitors observe the effects of the hidden system and infer its operation. Bell’s project does so explicitly by putting the system’s valves, pipes, gauges, and tanks directly on display.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice is unsupported because the passage says nothing about either creator celebrating or condemning artificiality.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice does not work because nothing suggests that the hydraulic events are impossible outside an artwork, and Bell is described as exposing the process, not merely recording it. D mischaracterizes Solano’s purpose; the text does not say she tries to imitate untouched nature.
choiceExplanations.D: This choice mischaracterizes Solano’s purpose; the text does not say she tries to imitate untouched nature.

questions.explanation:
Both projects draw visitors’ attention to infrastructure. Solano’s project does this implicitly: visitors observe the effects of the hidden system and infer its operation. Bell’s project does so explicitly by putting the system’s valves, pipes, gauges, and tanks directly on display.
B is unsupported because the passage says nothing about either creator celebrating or condemning artificiality.

choiceExplanations.B: This choice does not work because the underlined portion describes methods she successfully used rather than obstacles she encountered. C reverses the relationship: the project exemplifies, rather than departs from, her usual approach.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice reverses the relationship: the project exemplifies, rather than departs from, her usual approach.
choiceExplanations.D: The first sentence establishes a general claim: Okafor combines documentary research, chemical analysis, and spatial modeling. The underlined portion then supplies a concrete example, showing her using customs ledgers, strontium-isotope measurements, and shoreline maps together. questions.passage: Many premium agricultural products carry machine-readable seals whose microscopic patterns function as authenticity cues for automated customs scanners. Once calibrated, the scanners route packages displaying registered patterns through ordinary processing while diverting unrecognized ones for additional inspection. During a 2025 audit of saffron shipments, materials scientist Priya Menon and colleagues found that several uncertified packages containing dyed substitute fibers bore seal patterns closely resembling those on certified Kashmiri saffron containers. The researchers therefore concluded that _____
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the uncertified packages likely exploit a deceptive strategy in which products lacking certification reduce scrutiny by imitating an authenticity cue associated with certified goods.
choices.B: certified and uncertified saffron producers likely participate in a cooperative signaling system in which both groups benefit from displaying nearly identical seals.
choices.C: microscopic authentication seals are probably used more widely on fraudulent agricultural products than previous customs investigations have suggested.
choices.D: automated authentication is probably ineffective because customs scanners can readily distinguish registered seals from visually similar imitations.

choiceExplanations.A: This choice most directly follows from the evidence. The uncertified packages contain substitute material yet display patterns closely resembling the registered patterns that scanners use as evidence of authenticity. That is a deceptive imitation strategy: an unverified product gains an advantage by resembling a verified one. A contradicts the proposed benefit of the imitation and is not supported by any evidence that scanners reliably distinguish the counterfeit patterns.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice incorrectly treats the relationship as cooperative; the uncertified sellers are exploiting the signal rather than jointly benefiting from a legitimate shared certification system.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice makes an unsupported claim about how widespread such seals are across fraudulent products generally; the investigation concerns only the shipments examined.
choiceExplanations.D: This choice contradicts the proposed benefit of the imitation and is not supported by any evidence that scanners reliably distinguish the counterfeit patterns.

choices.A: continuing
choices.B: continue
choices.C: to have continued
choices.D: continued

choiceExplanations.C: This choice, “to have continued,” is an infinitive phrase and cannot serve as the sentence’s main verb in this construction.
choiceExplanations.D: This choice supplies the finite past-tense verb required by the sentence. The subject is the gerund phrase “collecting and reusing rooftop rainwater,” and the completed time span “From 2013 through 2023” calls for the past-tense verb “continued.” A, “continuing,” is a participle and leaves the sentence without a finite main verb.

The subject is the gerund phrase “collecting and reusing rooftop rainwater,” and the completed time span “From 2013 through 2023” calls for the past-tense verb “continued.” A, “continuing,” is a participle and leaves the sentence without a finite main verb. C, “to have continued,” is an infinitive phrase and cannot serve as the sentence’s main verb in this construction.
